newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 6.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Feb 6.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- US MERGER CREATES FINANCE GIANT

Morgan Stanley, the prestigious Wall Street investment bank, has announced a $24 billion merger with Dean Witter, a US retail financial services house. The deal, achieved by a share swap, will create the largest securities and investment banking firm in the US. The new group, in which Dean Witter shareholders have a 55 per cent controlling interest, will have annual revenues of $12 billion. Dean Witter's Discover credit card has 36 million US customers, making it the country's largest credit card issuer.
-- 1.9 BILLION STG PRU OFFER SETS UP SCOTAM BID WAR

A bidding war has opened for Scottish Amicable, the UK mutual life insurance giant which last week was the subject of a bid from Abbey National which valued the group at 1.4 billion stg. On Wednesday that bid was topped by Prudential Corporation, the UK's leading life insurer, whose offer values ScotAm at 1.9 billion stg. Abbey National has said it will reconsider improving its terms following the Prudential offer, and ScotAm has said it will seek a 'definitive offer' from Abbey National.
-- EUROTUNNEL TO PULL OUT OF CHANNEL PRICE-CUTTING WAR

Eurotunnel, the troubled operator of the Channel Tunnel, has indicated it is to pull out of the price-cutting battle for cross-Channel traffic. The price war has depressed earnings both at Eurotunnel and at the ferry companies. Announcing its intention to increase prices, Eurotunnel said it believed there would be a rationalisation of cross-Channel ferry services, and claimed that the proposed merger of ferry operators Stena Line and P&O, as well as the suspension of duty-free sales in the EU in 1999, would push up prices.
-- BOTTOMLEY SETS 'TOUGH' TOURISM TARGETS

Virginia Bottomley, the national heritage secretary, has unveiled a government strategy document which aims to increase Britain's earnings from tourism and create up to 1 million jobs in the industry over the next decade. The document, produced in partnership with the industry and tourism boards, sets tough growth targets for tourism. Bottomley confirmed that no new money would be forthcoming from the government to help meet the targets, but claimed there is huge potential for private sector investment, and said that National Lottery and Single Regeneration Budget sources could be tapped.
-- INSURERS URGED TO STOP USING GENETIC TEST RESULTS

The Association of British Insurers, the body representing Britain's insurance industry, has moved to relax the current controversial stance on genetic testing by urging its members not to use genetic test results to price mortgage-related life cover. Currently, nearly all insurance companies require customers to submit the results of genetic tests if they have taken them, although they do not propose compulsory testing. The responses from companies to the recommendation will be included in a document due to be published by the ABI later this month.
-- OFFER HOPES TO SOLVE GAS DILEMMA

The regulator of Britain's electricity industry, Professor Stephen Littlechild of Offer, has said that regional electricity companies will be consulted over the next few months over the issue of high-priced gas contracts. The companies are concerned over whether they will have to bear the brunt of the 15-year contracts, which date from the so-called 'dash for gas' in the early 1990's when gas prices were higher, or whether consumers will be able to subsidise them. Littlechild has said that consumer subsidy is one possible option, the other being a renegotiation of the contracts.
-- BSKYB MAY DROP KIRCH DEAL

Satellite broadcaster BSkyB has warned that unresolved 'important issues' are blocking progress in the company's plans to take a 49 per cent stake in German digital satellite operator DF-1. Seven months ago, BSkyB announced a strategic alliance with Kirche Gruppe, which runs DF-1. However, speaking on Wednesday, BSkyB chief executive Sam Chisholm said that 'some important issues need to be resolved. Until they are resolved we cannot proceed'. BSkyB announced pre-tax profits of 134 million stg for the six months to end-December, an increase of 26 per cent.
-- SAFEWAY IN TALKS WITH WELLWORTH

British supermarket chain Safeway is understood to be in talks about a possible joint venture with Northern Ireland's second largest supermarket chain. The British group is thought to be in talks with Fitzwilton, which owns 97 per cent of the Wellworth supermarket group. Wellworth currently has 21 per cent of the Northern Ireland market, and analysts estimate that a 50 per cent stake in the chain would cost Safeway between 90 million stg and 100 million stg.
-- BROKERS TO START 'GREY MARKET' IN BG AND CENTRICA

The Stock Market has granted approval to a proposal put forward by a number of City brokers to start a 'grey market' in the shares of BG plc and Centrica, the two companies that will be created by the planned demerger of British Gas on February 17. The grey market will begin next Monday, with the brokers, led by SG Warburg, claiming it will give some indication as to the future performance of shares in the two companies.
-- CONSUMER PRODUCTS LAUNCH HELPS BETACOM RIDE MARKET HURDLES

Telecommunications equipment and consumer electronics company Betacom has reported pre-tax profits in the six months to December 31 of 1.26 million stg, up from 257,000 stg, on sales ahead to 24.9 million stg (6.9 million stg). Betacom, which is majority-owned by Amstrad, said the 'significant upturn' in the results came despite fierce competition in the UK and depressed conditions in the continential European markets.
